extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), patent examiners, and advanced law students
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of doctrines that determine (1) when previously disclosed or used subject-matter is barred or dedicatied to the public, (2) when separate patents/applications are required or allowed (divisional, re-issue, joinder), and (3) how courts and the Patent Office differ in treating joinder and duplicative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedication/abandonment by public use or sale
rubrics_metrics.description: Dedication to the public of two years' public use or sale (or other acts indicating dedication) conclusively infers an intention to abandon the invention to the public and will cause loss of the monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law conclusively infers intent to abandon after such public use/sale and that inference cannot be overcome by evidence; the applicant, however, may in some cases prevent this inference by timely action (e.g., divisional filings). Cases cited include Adams v. Bellaire Stamping Co., Ex parte Derby, Ex parte Bohn. The text emphasizes the seriousness of public dedication and the need to act promptly to avoid loss of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Described-but-unclaimed matter in prior patent may be patentable (limited)
rubrics_metrics.description: Matter described but not claimed in a former patent is not necessarily a bar to later patenting unless it has been dedicated to the public; such matter may be the subject of a later patent in many authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule is qualified: courts differ, but many authorities hold that a subsequent patent may issue for matter described but unclaimed in a prior patent (see Suffolk Co. v. Hayden, Ex parte Emerson, Ex parte Derby). The doctrine is also tied to the two-year rule for process claims (see Eastern Paper Bag Co. v. Standard Paper Bag Co.). The relation to re-issue doctrine is noted: matter insertable in a re-issue may, if constituting a complete invention, be protected by a separate patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reservation clauses are disfavored (may mislead the public)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reservation clauses in an application (stating the right to claim inventions later) tend to mislead the public and should not be allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the subject-matter is properly divisible the inventor should file separate applications without reservation; when not divisible the second application must be filed while the first is pending or both may be adjudged together. Ex parte Blair (1888) is cited. The treatise warns reservations 'tend to mislead the public' and the Office/courts view them skeptically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of divisional or concurrent applications to avoid abandonment/dedication inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a second (divisional) application so that it is pending concurrently with the first anticipates and prevents the inference of dedication/abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant may expressly assert a reservation and should present and prosecute the second application without delay; filing so both are pending concurrently prevents the dedication inference. Cross-references and disclaimers may be used to clearly delineate limits of monopolies among related applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue vs separate patent where matter inseparable
rubrics_metrics.description: If new matter is inseparable from that already patented (i.e., cannot be separately claimed), a later patent covering it must fail and re-issue of the original may be the proper remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the later patent covers matter already protected by the prior patent (especially where the later claim is generic or broad), the later grant may be void; re-issue doctrine applies and in some cases the inventor must seek re-issue rather than a new patent. Authorities: Derby and other cases; re-issue considerations discussed in §§ 687-692, cross-referenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process and product (or machine and product) may be separately patented if separable
rubrics_metrics.description: A single inventive act that produces two concrete, truly separable results (e.g., a process and its product; a machine and the manufacture it creates) may give rise to separate patents for each if the inventions are truly separable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one patent necessarily covers the result of the other (duplication), the second patent cannot be granted (see Ex parte Holt; Mosler Safe & Lock Co. v. Mosler). When separable, cross-references should be inserted in each patent to distinguish them. Cases: Ex parte Lupton, Jones v. Sewall, Goodyear v. Providence Rubber Co., etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: No double-patenting for the same invention by the same inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Two patents cannot be granted to the same inventor for the same invention; likewise, two applications seeking patents for the same patentable subject-matter are objectionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventor who has filed an application cannot file another for the same concrete invention except as an amendment or after withdrawing prior matter; each application must show by proper allegations or disclaimers that its monopoly does not include subject-matter of the other. Related Ex parte decisions cited; the rule prevents duplicative monopolies and requires coordination between filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pending application claims bar later claims to same matter (limited)
rubrics_metrics.description: Matter claimed in a pending application by the same inventor cannot be claimed in a later application; after an application has passed to issue no other one covering the same matter should be passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are nuances: a second application will not be rejected merely because a prior one by same applicant is still pending (see Ex parte Gaboury); but matter already covered by a claim of a previous application is problematic (Ex parte Holt). The treatise notes tension between practices and the need for disclaimers/cross-claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder in courts: kindred/auxiliary inventions may be joined
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts permit joinder of several inventions in one patent where the inventions are kindred and auxiliary — capable of being used in connection to serve a common end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'kindred and auxiliary' test: if inventions are cognate, relate to same invention and same subject and have a common object/purpose, claims can be made in same patent. Courts historically more liberal; examples and authority: Densmore v. Schofield, Hogg v. Emerson, Wyeth v. Stone. But separate and independent inventions without a common connected use cannot be joined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder in Patent Office: dependency and single result required
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office permits joinder of distinct inventions in one application only where one invention is dependent on the other and they mutually contribute to produce a single result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office applies classification and operational tests: inventions in absolutely distinct classes or unrelated in design/operation should be divided; dependent/auxiliary inventions or intimately connected parts that cooperate to produce the result may be joined. Ex parte Young, Ex parte Freese, Ex parte Gokey cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and divisional requirement in the Patent Office
rubrics_metrics.description: An application should not ordinarily embrace matters belonging to absolutely distinct, independent, and unconnected official classes or sub-classes; in such cases a division should be insisted upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification of the arts (Office groups) matters — if inventions belong to different statutory classes they cannot be joined unless inseparable. The Office may require division to avoid repeated examination in different divisions and to maintain organized records. Ex parte Mefford, Ex parte Herr discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-disclaimers and cross-references between related applications
rubrics_metrics.description: When two pending applications describe the same general invention but only one claims it, the one not claiming must disclaim and refer to the other by date and number; cross-disclaimers are required in two pending applications for the same general invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requirement for cross-disclaimers is largely directory but customary; it helps clarify limits of each monopoly. The Office may insist on disclaimers to show limits and to avoid conflicting grants, but the failure to do so is not always fatal in the courts (see Ex parte Blair, Ex parte Finch, Ex parte Roberts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of misjoinder: invalidation if parts are independent and one is not new
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent joins separate and independent inventions (not connected in design or operation) the patent may be void because joining what cannot lawfully be united risks invalidation (if one part is not new or is dedicated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise warns that joinder of unrelated inventions can lead to perilous consequences: if any one of the supposed inventions was known or dedicated, the patent could be void in whole under common-law doctrines. Courts sometimes nonetheless sustain patents to protect parties, but the Patent Office takes a stricter approach to avoid such results.
